The research was carried out under a NASA Aeronautics Research Institute (NARI) funded project.
The objective was to evaluate emerging materials and manufacturing technologies to enable fully non-metallic gas turbine engines.
The system analysis estimated a 4.9% reduction in fuel burn and 7.7% increase in landing-takeoff NOx margin for the advanced engine with PMCs and CMCs.
PMCs were envisioned for use in the inlet acoustic duct, fan stator, and first four rows of the high-pressure compressor vanes.
CMCs were used in the combustor liner, high-pressure turbine vanes/blades, low-pressure turbine vanes/blades, and core nozzle.

The use of CMCs enabled the elimination of all turbine blade and vane cooling, leading to a 1.5 point efficiency improvement in the high-pressure turbine and 0.5 point improvement in the low-pressure turbine.
The IGVs were tested in a wind tunnel cascade at velocities ranging from 100 to 600 ft/s and angles from 0 to 60 degrees.
The maximum displacement of the IGVs increased with increasing velocity and angle of incidence, with the ABS vane with baseline fillet having the largest displacement up to several millimeters.
No fracture was detected in the IGVs, even at the 'closed' 90 degree position.
Acoustic liners were fabricated using Fused Deposition Modeling, including a conventional Helmholtz design and an advanced 'Passive-Destructive' design.
The acoustic liners were tested in the NASA Langley Grazing Flow Impedance Tube.
An acoustically-treated access panel for a turbofan engine bypass duct was also fabricated using additive manufacturing.
Detailed experimental results of the polymer composite process development and characterization are described in the second report.
The ceramic matrix composite components included the high pressure turbine second stage nozzle and the high pressure turbine shroud for auxiliary power units.
The high pressure turbine nozzle was chosen as it is a static structural component subjected to high temperatures but in a relatively low stress environment.
